Alzheimer's disease Autophagy Fatty acids Glycomics Microbiota Neurodegeneration Gut Microbiota Impact on Neurodegenerative Diseases Introduction Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a degenerative disease of the central nervous system. It represents the leading cause of dementia worldwide, impacting over 50 million people. AD symptoms include memory loss, cognitive deficits in areas such as language, abstract thinking, orientation, and alterations in behavior, such as mobility loss [ 1 , 2 ]. Two classical neuropathological features of AD include amyloid plaques formed by the deposition of misfolded β-amyloid (Aβ) in the brain and neurofibrillary tangles caused by Tau protein hyperphosphorylation [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ]. In addition, the etiology and pathogenesis of AD are dependent on several factors, including internal factors, such as fragile immunologic barrier and nervous system, disturbed circadian rhythm, series of cellular and organellar dysfunction, etc., and external factors, such as imbalanced diet and lifestyle, chronic stress, the constitution of gut microbiota, etc [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ]. Due to the intricate mechanisms driving its pathogenesis and pathophysiology, effective clinical treatments for this condition remain elusive. Owing to its consumption of high levels of energy, the brain is highly vulnerable to impaired energy metabolism and oxidative stress; even minor changes in signal transduction and metabolism can have a significant impact [ 13 , 14 ]. For example, gut-derived molecules, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) digested from fat, could be translocated from the gut to the brain and modulate the immune functions of microglia, promoting Aβ plaque deposition. Recent studies have demonstrated that SCFA levels in cerebrospinal fluid can potentially be used as biomarkers of NDs [ 15 , 16 , 17 ]. SCFAs can enter mitochondria without the help of membrane transporters, and then can be oxidized by the enzymes that are located in the mitochondrial matrix [ 18 ]. In such scenarios, it is crucial to maintain a healthy and dynamic pool of mitochondria to ensure the brain’s longevity and high energy demands. Since brain cells are post-mitotic, they depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for energy production [ 16 , 19 ]. The intracerebral pathology of AD often leads to impaired morphology and functions of neuronal mitochondria [ 20 , 21 , 22 ]. The quality of a healthy mitochondrial network relies on the unintermittent mobilizing and distribution of mitochondria to meet the high energy demands of long-living neurons, indicating that continuous changes in mitochondrial fusion and fission, and mitophagy are indispensable [ 23 ]. Both clinically and experimentally, researchers have found changes expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fusion, fission, and mitophagy in response to the pathological process of AD [ 24 , 25 ]. The mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 is overactivated in AD patient brains, AD mouse white matter, and mature oligodendrocytes exposed to toxic Aβ peptides. Loss of Drp1 affects normal dendritic and axonal development and mobility of neuronal mitochondria. Previous studies have shown that DRP1 abundance increases with the progression of AD. Furthermore, Drp1 inhibition in AD models ameliorated cognitive deficits, synaptic plasticity impairment, and Aβ deposition [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ]. Another protein, PINK1/PARKIN, plays a significant role in mitophagy and regulates various signaling processes, including ubiquitination and phosphorylation, essential for the removal of impaired mitochondria [ 30 , 31 ]. However, PINK1/PARKIN signaling is highly disrupted in models of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Furthermore, overexpression of PINK1/PARKIN has been shown to improve mitophagy in AD models, which is beneficial in maintaining the mitochondrial dynamic [ 32 , 33 , 34 ]. The gut microbiota is considered crucial for human brain development, physiology, and body metabolism [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ]. Fecal microbiota transplantation trials have demonstrated the therapeutic effects of a healthy microbiota [ 39 , 40 , 41 ]. Located in the human gut, Akkermansia muciniphila , which serves as a mucin- and SCFA-yielding microorganism is essential for gut homeostasis [ 42 ]. Propionic acid is one of the main metabolites of Akkermansia muciniphila [ 43 ]. The present study evaluated the protective effects of propionic acid and Akkermansia muciniphila in the AD mice model. Their impacts on neuronal mitochondrial morphology, fission, and mitophagy were examined both in vitro and in vivo. Our findings offer new avenues in the field of mitochondrial research in neurodegeneration models, providing a novel perspective on AD treatment targeted on diet and gut-brain axis (GBA) intervention. Results Reduced serum and fecal propionic acid levels in AD patients We conducted GC–MS analysis to determine absolute quantification of six critical SCFAs in fecal and serum samples obtained from 19 AD patients and 18 healthy volunteers. Our findings revealed that the levels of propionic acid ( p < 0.0001) and n-butyric acid ( p < 0.0001) were substantially reduced in the fecal samples of AD patients in comparison to the healthy controls (Fig. 1 A and D). There were no significant intergroup differences in the fecal levels of acetic, isobutyric, isovaleric, and n-valeric acids (Fig. 1 B-C and E-F). Furthermore, we observed significantly lower serum levels of n-butyric ( p < 0.005) and propionic acids ( p < 0.0002) in AD patients than in normal healthy controls (Fig. 1 G and J). Serum levels of acetic, isobutyric, isovaleric, and n-valeric acids did not differ significantly between the two groups (Fig. 1H-I and K-L). Propionic acid improves cognitive dysfunction in AD mice model To further investigate whether propionic acid impacts AD progression, the AD mice model was fed with sodium propionate (SP)-containing drinking water for 8 weeks (Fig. 2 A). The intervention with SP yielded a notable elevation in propionic acid levels within both serum (Fig. 2 B) and cerebrospinal fluid (Fig. 2 C) of 5 × FAD mice in comparison to their untreated counterparts. In contrast, the levels of acetic, isobutyric, butyric, isovaleric, and valeric acids of 5 × FAD mice were not significantly different compared to those of controls (Figures S1A-J). In addition, SP treatment did not affect body weight, daily food intake, and daily water intake of mice (Figures S2A-B). According to the results of the Morris water maze test, 5 × FAD mice took more time to reach the hidden platform on days 3 and 5 and spent significantly less time and distance in the target quadrant compared to WT mice (Fig. 2 D and G-H), indicating impaired learning and memory functions in 5 × FAD mice. It is noteworthy that compared to untreated 5 × FAD mice, SP-treated 5 × FAD mice spent a longer time in the target quadrant (Fig. 2 G-H). Thus, these findings indicated that SP treatment enhanced the preference of 5 × FAD mice for the location of the target platform (Fig. 2 E), shortening the delay in reaching the hidden platform (Fig. 2 D). The results of the open field test showed that SP treatment led to a reduction in the area of activity of the 5 × FAD mice in the central region, the mice’s motor function was not altered (Fig. 2I-K). The results of the elevated plus maze test also demonstrated that SP treatment resulted in the reduction of the activity time and the distance in the open-arm region of the 5 × FAD mice model (Figures S2C-F). The Open field test and Morris water maze test did not show any substantial difference in the total distance traveled or movement speed among the various groups of mice (Fig. 2 F and K-L), indicating normal motor function in all experimental groups. Taken together, the findings indicated that SP treatment significantly improved the spatial learning and memory of the 5 × FAD mice. Propionic acid improves the mitochondrial function of HT22 cells For in vitro experiments, we used HT22 cells as a hippocampal neuron model. The optimal dose of SP was evaluated by cell viability using CCK8 assay (Figure S3A-C). Compared to untreated controls, we observed significantly lower cell proliferation (Fig. 3 A) and ATP production (Fig. 3 C) and a significantly higher intracellular accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Fig. 3 B) in HT22 cells treated with 40 µM of Aβ oligomers. However, pretreatment with 5 mM SP significantly reversed the Aβ-induced effects (Fig. 3 A-C). We also examined the mitochondrial membrane potential in Aβ-treated cells after SP treatment with mito tracker staining. Representative fluorescent images are shown in Fig. 3 D, Aβ intervention had a tendency to reduce fluorescence intensity in HT22 cells, SP treatment rescue the reduce of mito tracker fluorescence intensity induced by Aβ. Taken together, these results suggest that SP decreased Aβ toxicity and oxidative stress-induced damage. Meanwhile, we focused on the expression levels of genes related to mitochondrial division, mitochondrial fusion, mitochondrial mitophagy, mitochondrial production, and synaptic plasticity (Fig. 3 E-K). We found that Aβ challenge induce mitochondrial over fission and reduction on mitochondrial fusion in HT22 cells, suggesting that intervention targeting mitochondrial fission and fusion homeostasis may be a potential approach in AD prevention. Aβ treatment caused the post-synaptic membrane protein and synaptophysin mRNA expression was reduced by Aβ treatment, and this was rescued by propionate pretreatment. GPR41 and GPR43 expression was significantly increased by adding SP to the cell culture medium (Fig. 3 L-M). These results suggest that SP improved mitochondrial function, ATP production and synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons which may contribute to neuronal recovery from Aβ-induced toxicity. Propionic acid improves mitochondrial division and mitophagy in the hippocampus of 5 × FAD mice To elucidate the mechanisms underlying the improvement of mitochondrial function post-SP treatment, we performed western blotting and real-time PCR to assess the expression of genes related to mitochondrial function. Compared to WT mice, we observed higher levels of protein Drp1 in the hippocampus of 5 × FAD mice, along with lower levels of Pink1 . However, it did not alter the expression of the mitochondrial mitophagy protein PARKIN (Fig. 4 A-D). Our findings demonstrated that SP treatment partially reduced Drp1 mRNA expression in the hippocampus and enhanced Pink1 mRNA expression (Fig. 4 E-G). Furthermore, immunofluorescence analysis showed that SP treatment reduced the expression of Drp1 in the dentate gyrus (DG) region of the hippocampus (Fig. 4 H) and an increase in Pink1 expression (Fig. 4 I), while PARKIN protein expression remained unchanged. However, co-localization analyses revealed that, compared to WT mice, 5 × FAD mice exhibited a reduction in the co-localization of the PARKIN protein with outer mitochondrial membrane protein TOM20. SP treatment of the 5 × FAD mice normalized the co-localization of PARKIN with TOM20 (Fig. 4 J), which indicated that SP treatment led to the enhancement of PARKIN recruitment in mitochondria, enhancing mitochondrial mitophagy in hippocampal neurons. To further investigate the effect of propionic acid on mitochondrial function, we next observed the mitochondrial morphology using transmission electron microscopy. We found significant mitochondrial vacuolization and a lack of mitochondrial cristae in the mitochondria of the hippocampal neurons of 5 × FAD mice. In contrast, for 5 × FAD mice treated with SP, we observed the presence of mitochondrial cristae and aggregation of endoplasmic reticulum into the damaged mitochondria in the hippocampal neurons (Fig. 4 K). We also found that SP treatment led to a significant increase in the thickness of the postsynaptic dense zone, which indicated that SP improved synaptic plasticity, while there was no significant intergroup difference in the synaptic gaps (Fig. 4 L-N). Propionic acid improves mitochondrial division and mitophagy in HT22 cells via GPR41 and GPR43 It is now known that propionic acid primarily acts via G protein-coupled receptor-mediated signaling, wherein GPR41 and GPR43 receptors are critically involved [ 44 ]. To further investigate the mechanisms underlying the regulation of mitochondrial function, HT22 cells were treated with GPR41 inhibitor (SHB) and GPR43 inhibitor (GLPG0974) [ 45 ] or three shRNA lentiviruses for GPR41 and GPR43 (Fig. 5 ). Our results from Western blotting and RT-qPCR demonstrated that SP inhibited Drp1 expression in a GPR41-dependent manner and enhanced Pink1 expression through GPR43 receptors (Fig. 5 A-N). The immunofluorescence results revealed that the GPR43 receptor exhibits a propensity to facilitate the accumulation of PARKIN within mitochondria, thereby augmenting mitophagy (Fig. 5 O). In Aβ-treated HT22 cells, we observed that the mitochondria exhibited a significant loss of mitochondrial cristae, an increase in mitochondrial vacuolization, and no endoplasmic reticulum aggregation to mitochondria. On the other hand, in the cells pre-treated with propionic acid, we observed the presence of mitochondrial cristae and aggregation of endoplasmic reticulum in damaged mitochondria. When the GPR43 receptor was knocked down, the ameliorative effect of propionic acid on mitochondrial mitophagy was eliminated, and the endoplasmic reticulum no longer aggregated in the damaged mitochondria (Fig. 5 P). SP improves mitochondrial mitophagy in mouse hippocampus via GRP43 and mitochondrial division via GRP41 To further confirm the mechanisms underlying the protective effects of propionic acid on 5 × FAD, 2.5 months old 5 × FAD mice were stereotaxically injected with lentivirus shGPR41, shGPR43, or shControl (empty vector) in the hippocampal DG region. At 3.5 months of age, the mice were orally administered SP through their drinking water, and at 5.5 months of age, the mice were euthanized, and samples were collected for molecular testing (Fig. 6 A) and analysis of shRNA knockdown effects (Fig. 6 B and C). Western blotting and RT-qPCR results showed that hippocampal Drp1 expression was significantly higher in AD mice compared to WT mice. Furthermore, hippocampal Drp1 expression was significantly lower in SP-treated 5 × FAD mice compared to the untreated 5 × FAD mice. However, there was no significant difference in the Drp1 expression of untreated 5 × FAD mice and 5 × FAD mice treated with lentivirus shGPR41 and SP (Fig. 6 D-E), demonstrating that the ameliorative effect of propionic acid on the mitochondrial division was mediated via the GPR41 receptor. Hippocampal Pink1 expression was significantly lower in 5 × FAD mice compared to the WT mice. Moreover, hippocampal Pink1 expression was significantly higher in the 5 × FAD mice treated with SP compared to the 5 × FAD group. However, there was no significant difference in the Pink1 expression of untreated 5 × FAD mice and 5 × FAD mice treated with lentivirus shGPR43 and SP (Fig. 6 D, G, and H), demonstrating that the ameliorative effect of propionic acid on mitochondrial mitophagy was mediated via the GPR43 receptor. The results of the immunofluorescence analysis in the DG region of the mouse hippocampus were consistent with the results of western blotting and RT-qPCR. More importantly, we found SP treatment led to an increase in the co-localization region of PARKIN and TOM20. But for 5 × FAD mice infected with lentivirus shGPR43, SP treatment could no longer increase the co-localization region of PARKIN and TOM20 (Fig. 6 I). Our findings demonstrated that the mitochondria in the hippocampal neurons of 5 × FAD mice exhibited notably increased mitochondrial division, a lack of mitochondrial cristae, vacuolization of mitochondria, and no aggregation of the endoplasmic reticulum. However, in SP-treated 5 × FAD mice, mitochondrial cristae could be detected in the mitochondria of the hippocampal neurons. The appearance of the mitochondrial cristae and the aggregation of the endoplasmic reticulum in the damaged mitochondria indicated the induction of mitochondrial mitophagy (Fig. 6 J). These findings indicated that SP treatment improves mitochondrial mitophagy in hippocampal neurons through activation of GPR43 and hippocampal mitochondrial division in 5 × FAD mice through activation of GPR41. SP reduces Drp1 expression and inhibits neuronal mitochondrial hyperdivision by suppressing Erk phosphorylation Previous studies have shown that Erk is an upstream regulatory gene of Drp1 [ 46 ]. In the current study, western blotting revealed that SP treatment in HT22 cells led to significant inhibition of phosphorylated ERK (p-ERK) (Fig. 6 K and L). Furthermore, treatment of HT22 cells with ERK inhibitor U0126 led to Drp1 downregulation (Fig. 5 A and C). The results of in vivo studies showed that ERK phosphorylation levels were significantly higher in 5 × FAD mice than in WT mice and that oral administration of SP reduced p-ERK levels in the hippocampal region of mice. There was no difference in the ERK phosphorylation levels when shGPR41 was injected into the DG region of mice hippocampus; however, shGPR43 injection reduced p-ERK expression (Fig. 6 M and N), demonstrating that SP reduces Drp1 expression by decreasing ERK phosphorylation, thereby suppressing neuronal mitochondrial hyperdivision. SP reduces blood–brain barrier permeability in AD mice The blood–brain barrier is compromised in individuals with AD and transgenic animal models of AD [ 47 ]. To further evaluate the protective effect of SP in AD cases, we analyzed the blood–brain barrier permeability in 5 × FAD mice using Evens Blue. Our study revealed that SP had a tendency to reduce blood–brain barrier permeability in 5 × FAD mice (Figure S4A). Additionally, we established in vitro blood–brain barrier models on Transwell utilizing human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMEC), human brain vascular pericytes (HBVP), and human astrocytes (HA1800). The in vitro blood–brain barrier models were analyzed using Fluorescein sodium and Teer. Our results showed that SP treatment could potentially reverse the Aβ-induced impairment of the blood–brain barrier (Figures S4B-C). The levels of a tight junction protein, Occludin, in HBMEC were detected using RT-qPCR. Our findings showed that SP treatment led to the upregulation of occludin (OCLN) mRNA (Figure S4D). The above results suggest the potential of SP treatment to improve blood–brain barrier permeability in AD models. However, SP treatment alone (without Aβ) reduced the mRNA expression of occludin. The gut microbiota of AD patients differs from that of healthy individuals Alterations in the composition of the gut microbiota have been associated with several human diseases, including AD. An individual’s gut microbiota plays a vital role in maintaining the host’s metabolic homeostasis, and metabolites originating from the gut microbiota also impact the signaling pathways involved in the activities of the central nervous system (CNS) [ 48 ]. To determine the differences in the gut microbiota of AD patients and that of healthy individuals, we analyzed the gut microbiota composition of 19 AD patients and 18 healthy volunteers using the 16S rRNA gene. None of these individuals had taken antibiotics in the past two months and did not have any major metabolic or chronic diseases. Different diversity indices (Chao1 estimator, observed species richness, Shannon’s diversity index, Simpson’s index, Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, Pielou’s evenness index, and Good’s nonparametric coverage estimator) were used to assess the diversity of the gut microbiota. We found that compared to healthy individuals, we observed a significant decrease in Chao1 estimate, observed species richness, Shannon’s diversity index, Simpson’s index, and Pielou’s evenness index of AD patients ( P = 0.0043, 0.0052, 0.00093, 0.0017, and 0.00042, respectively; Fig. 7 A). Principal component analysis (PCA) of microbiome-based bacterial communities and PCoA plots of weighted UniFraq distance matrices revealed significant differences in gut microbiota beta diversity of AD patients compared to that of healthy individuals (Figs. 7 C-D). Rarefaction curves showed extensive biodiversity coverage (Fig. 7 B). The phylum-level relative abundance histogram shows the difference in dominant species between AD patients and healthy controls, with AD patients showing more Proteobacteria (Fig. 7 E). Absolute quantification of Akkermansia muciniphila levels in AD patients and healthy individuals revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila levels were significantly lower in AD patients than in healthy individuals (Fig. 7 F). Akkermansia muciniphila protects against cognitive dysfunction in AD mice We hypothesized that compared to healthy individuals, AD patients suffered from lower proportions of Akkermansia muciniphila in the intestinal flora, resulting in lower levels of its metabolite propionic acid and a lack of the patient’s ability to resist cognitive dysfunction. To test this hypothesis, the experimental group of mice was supplemented with Akkermansia muciniphila via oral gavage for 8 weeks at 3.5 months of age, while the mice in the control group were gavaged with saline. Behavioral assays were performed at 5.5 months of age, followed by euthanasia for molecular analysis (Fig. 8 A). No significant intergroup differences were found in food intake, water intake, body weight, and blood glucose levels (Figures S5A-C, J). However, we observed a significant increase in the levels of propionic acid in the experimental group (Fig. 8 B). The remaining differences in short-chain fatty acid content remained consistent (Figures S5E-I), and there was a notable rise in fecal Akkermansia muciniphila content after gavage (Figures S5D). Behavioral assessments demonstrated that AD mice had notably lower nesting scores than control mice, but Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation significantly improved their nesting scores (Fig. 8 D-E). In the water maze experiment, compared to the untreated AD mice, Akkermansia muciniphila -treated AD mice spent longer time and distance in the target quadrant (Fig. 8 J-K), crossed the target platform more often (Fig. 8 I), had a preference for the location of the target platform (Fig. 8 G), and had a shorter delay in reaching the hidden platform (Fig. 8 F). In the new object recognition test, we found no change in the total time spent visiting new or old objects after supplementation with Akkermansia muciniphila and an increase in the ratio of the number of times AD mice were exposed to new objects/total number of times they were exposed to objects (Fig. 8 L-N). The above experiments demonstrated that Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation significantly reversed cognitive dysfunction and spatial memory loss in 5 × FAD mice, which might be attributed to the increase in the levels of the metabolite propionic acid. Akkermansia muciniphila protects hippocampal mitochondrial division and mitophagy homeostasis in 5 × FAD mice We performed western blotting to detect the expression of the genes related to mitochondrial function. We found that Akkermansia muciniphila treatment in mice partially reduced the expression of Drp1 in the hippocampus and enhanced the expression of Pink1 , but did not alter the expression of the mitochondrial mitophagy protein PARKIN (Fig. 9 A-D). Similarly, immunofluorescence results revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila treatment of the DG region of the hippocampus partially enhanced the expression of Pink1 (Fig. 9 E). Co-localization investigations demonstrated that treatment with Akkermansia muciniphila resulted in an increased co-localization region of PARKIN and TOM20 (Fig. 9 F). This suggests that Akkermansia muciniphila treatment enhances mitochondrial mitophagy in hippocampal neurons and improves hippocampal mitochondrial division in 5 × FAD mice. To further investigate the effects of Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation on mitochondrial function, we next observed the morphology of mouse hippocampal mitochondria using transmission electron microscopy and found that mitochondria in hippocampal neurons of 5 × FAD mice showed significant loss of mitochondrial cristae, vacuolation of mitochondria, and lack of endoplasmic reticulum aggregation to mitochondria. However, Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation reversed the lack of mitochondrial cristae in neurons (Fig. 9 G). We also found that it led to a significant increase in the thickness of the postsynaptic dense zone, while there were no significant intergroup differences in the synaptic gaps (Figs. 9 H-J). These findings demonstrated that Akkermansia muciniphila exerted a similar protective effect as its metabolite propionic acid in the 5 × FAD model. Histological sections of the heart, liver, kidney, spleen, and lung of each group of mice were stained with HE to observe pathological changes, and Alcian blue staining showed that Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation did not impair the thickness of the colonic mucus layer (Fig. 9 K-L). We found that Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation did not significantly affect the heart, liver, kidney, spleen, lung, and colonic mucosal layer of the mice (Figures S6A-F). Discussion This study reveals the protective mechanism of microbiota-derived propionic acid against Alzheimer’s disease at three levels: in elderly patients, in model mice, and in cells. Also, it demonstrates for the first time that pre-intervention of GPR41 and GPR43-mediated neuronal mitochondrial division and autophagy improves cognitive function in Alzheimer’s disease model mice. This effect was produced by a GPR41-mediated decrease in Drp1 expression and a GPR43-mediated increase in Pink1 expression and Parkin movement to the mitochondria. The novelty of our study lies in demonstrating that cognitive impairment in Alzheimer’s disease model mice can be alleviated solely by restoring mitochondrial dynamics homeostasis and autophagy, without the need for direct intervention in amyloid peptide or tau phosphorylation, although we cannot rule out potential effects on the amyloid and tau pathways. Figure 10 summarizes the mechanism of propionic acid in regulating neuronal mitochondrial homeostasis and emphasizes the potential role of microbiota-derived SCFAs in the prevention of NDs. The preventive effect of SCFAs, a class of metabolites of intestinal flora, on AD is well known [ 49 , 50 ]. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the protective effect of propionic acid AD cases remain unclear [ 51 ]. Some studies have shown that propionic acid can prevent Alzheimer’s disease by increasing gliosis [ 52 ], but there are few reports on HT22. In addition, higher propionic acid levels in serum are positively correlated with higher cognitive levels [ 53 ]. In Parkinson’s disease, fecal propionic acid content is less than in healthy controls [ 54 ]. Our study demonstrated that propionic acid administration before the onset of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) could ameliorate cognitive impairments in mice and cellular models. Furthermore, our findings suggest that SP may slow down AD progression, partially through mitochondria-mediated modifications in SP-activated receptors in hippocampal neuronal cells Previous studies have demonstrated that the post-mortem brains of AD patients exhibited impaired mitochondrial morphology and dynamics as well as defective energy metabolism [ 55 ]. Another study showed that AD patients and mice models exhibit an imbalance between mitochondrial fission and fusion (increased fission and decreased fusion) [ 56 ]. Furthermore, the mitochondrial division has been shown to be primarily regulated by Drp1 [ 57 ]. The AD progression-restricting activity of propionic acid is primarily mediated via either of the two free fatty acid receptors: GPR43 or GPR41 [ 58 ]. In this study, our results showed that SP treatment led to GPR41-mediated downregulation of Drp1 expression in mouse hippocampal neurons. Recent studies have revealed that there are two types of Drp1 -mediated fission in mitochondria, with divisions in the periphery shedding damaged material into smaller mitochondria and divisions in the middle region leading to the proliferation of mitochondria [ 59 ]. However, which type of mitochondrial fission is mediated by Drp1 overexpression in AD patients remains unknown. We did not use Seahorse to assay mitochondrial function in the mouse hippocampus, but we believe that we have elucidated part of the mechanism of propionic acid and mitochondrial fission mitophagy through behavior and pathology. Mitochondrial mitophagy is a protective cellular process that inhibits ROS formation. Impaired mitochondrial mitophagy is a crucial factor in aging, especially in individuals with neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Recent studies suggest that deficiencies in mitochondrial mitophagy may arise before beta-amyloid accumulation during the progression of AD [ 60 ]. Targeting the mitochondrial mitophagy pathway has been proposed as a potential therapeutic modality to counter AD progression [ 61 ]. PINK1/PARKIN deficiency has been shown to exacerbate cognitive dysfunction in AD mice [ 62 ]; however, overexpression of proteins associated with mitochondrial mitophagy has been shown to improve these phenotypes [ 63 ]. In the current study, we found that AD mice exhibited a deficiency of neuronal Pink1 , whereas SP treatment alleviated Pink1 levels in AD mice and HT22 cells via the GPR43 receptor. We found that Parkin expression remained unaffected in AD mice and HT22 cells; however, PARKIN was unable to translocate to mitochondria to mediate its Mitophagy function. Previous studies have shown that accumulation of Tau protein in neuroblastoma cells and cryptobacterial models leads to inhibition of mitochondrial mitophagy by reducing Parkin translocation in mitochondria [ 64 ].. In the current study, we found that PARKIN was unable to recruit mitochondria in AD mice and hippocampal neuronal cell models with β-amyloid hyperload. SP treatment triggered PARKIN aggregation in mitochondria via the GPR43 receptor. The relationship between the loss of mitochondrial function and cognitive dysfunction needs to be further investigated. Recently, it has been suggested that ROS-induced mitochondrial damage might be closely related to neuronal survival, and protection of mitochondria against ROS accumulation can help maintain normal mitochondrial function and cognitive function [ 65 ]. It has also been indicated that mitochondrial integrity, cortical connectivity, and antioxidant-mediated restoration of cognitive behavior make oxidative stress a potential therapeutic target for NDs [ 66 ]. To the best of our knowledge, this was the first study demonstrating that the maintenance of hippocampal neuronal mitochondrial function (normal fusion homeostasis and mitochondrial mitophagy) in AD patients might help protect both cognitive functions. Defective blood–brain barrier integrity and impaired memory [ 67 ], and language functions [ 68 ] are closely associated with NDs, such as AD [ 47 ]. The intestinal microbiota influences the permeability of the blood–brain barrier (BBB). Studies on germ-free versus specific pathogen-free mice have emphasized the potential role of SCFAs in maintaining BBB integrity. Germ-free animals exhibited increased BBB permeability and disruption of brain endothelial tight junctions [ 69 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated the beneficial protective effects of propionic acid, a SCFA, on the blood–brain barrier, alleviating harmful inflammation and oxidative stimulation [ 58 ]; however, the protective effect of propionic acid on blood–brain barrier damage in AD cases has been rarely reported. In the current study, we believe that propionic acid has the potential to enhance the integrity of the blood–brain barrier and the expression of tight junction proteins, the exact mechanism of which needs to be further investigated. To the best of our knowledge, our study provides the initial insight into the protective effects of SP concerning Alzheimer’s disease (AD), demonstrating a novel approach using metabolites derived from the gut microbiota. In addition, reduced SCFAs production in the gut, either due to dietary changes or reduced levels of gut microbiota, has been found to lead to impaired Treg cell function in animal models of autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and type 1 diabetes [ 70 , 71 , 72 ]. In multiple sclerosis patients, propionic acid has been postulated to improve inhibitory Treg cell function [ 73 ]. In Parkinson’s disease, SCFAs have been shown to act as neuroprotective and/or neuromodulators through epigenetic regulation [ 74 ]. It has also been suggested that increased production of microbial propionic acid, which might activate FFAR3 in gut neurons, exerts a protective effect against the progression of Parkinson’s disease [ 75 ]. Therefore, the mechanisms underlying the protective roles of gut microbiota-derived propionic acid in the pathophysiology of NDs might be complex. Here, we identify only a few potential pathways through which propionic acid exerts its protective role in AD, and the remaining potential pathways remain to be investigated. The concentration of propionic acid used in this study was higher than physiological levels. Previous studies have demonstrated that even lower concentrations of propionic acid can enhance mitochondrial function and mitigate neurodegeneration in neurons [ 76 , 77 , 78 ]. We selected a higher concentration primarily to compensate for propionic acid’s volatility and to ensure consistent exposure throughout the cell experiments. Given the link between changes in the gut microbiota and variations in brain activity, the gut microbiome has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Modulation of the microbiota through various methods, such as probiotics, prebiotics therapy, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), has shown potential to alleviate cognitive impairments in individuals with AD [ 79 , 80 , 81 , 82 ]. Several studies now suggest that the gut microbiome helps maintain normal cognitive function by regulating innate and adaptive immunity [ 83 , 84 ], stimulating the vagus nerve [ 85 ], and affecting the peripheral and central nervous system by other approaches. Very few studies have reported the effects of SCFAs, metabolites of the gut microbiome, on mitochondrial function in AD neurons. At the same time, most available data from animal studies relate only to the late pathological stages of AD, and few researchers have focused on the early stages of AD pathogenesis [ 86 ]. Our analyses involving microbial and SP interventions in mice before AD onset revealed that modulation of mitochondrial function during the early stages of AD onset could be a potential therapeutic avenue to improve the outcome of individuals suffering from NDs. Using 16 s rDNA sequencing, we detected significant differences in the structure, abundance, and diversity of the gut microbiome of AD patients and healthy individuals. Moreover, the abundance of Proteobacteria in AD patients was significantly higher than that in healthy volunteers, which were consistent with previous studies [ 87 , 88 ]. However, recent studies propose that modifications in the proportions of specific microorganisms do not necessarily reflect changes in the structure of the gut microbiota and their effects on the host. Studies that focus on relative proportions of specific microbes often ignore the possibility that changes in the overall microbial abundance per se might be a major cause behind the underlying disease of the host, indicating the significance of absolute levels of microbiota [ 89 , 90 ]. SCFAs are the metabolites of the intestinal microbiota produced by the fermentation of indigestible carbohydrates [ 91 ]. Akkermansia muciniphila is one of the representative intestinal microorganisms that produce propionic acid as a metabolite [ 92 , 93 ]. In the current study, we found that the absolute levels of Akkermansia muciniphila were significantly lower in AD patients than in healthy individuals. Although we did not directly observe a correlation between reduced Akkermansia muciniphila levels and lower propionic acid concentrations in clinical samples, we found in a mouse model that oral administration of A. muciniphila led to increased propionic acid levels in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Given A. muciniphila’s ability to produce propionic acid, this suggests that the elevated promotion propionic acid levels in the model animals were a consequence of A. muciniphila supplementation. A previous study reported that Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation slowed down the pathological changes in the brains of high-fat diet-fed APP/PS1 mice and alleviated spatial learning and memory deficit through the management of metabolic disorders [ 43 ]. However, our study did not reveal any substantial impact of Akkermansia muciniphila supplementation on the metabolism of 5 × FAD mice fed a normal diet. Nonetheless, it was hypothesized that it could improve cognitive dysfunction through the repair of neuronal mitochondrial function mediated by propionic acid. These inconsistent results might be attributed to diet, mice age, and the Akkermansia muciniphila gavage cycle. In conclusion, our study revealed the beneficial effects of supplementation of propionic acid and enterobacterial Akkermansia muciniphila as early intervention in AD models, thus, targeting mitochondrial dysfunction via gut microbiota and its metabolites might open a new avenue for neurodegenerative disease early intervention. Methods Participants We recruited a total of 19 patients with positive amyloid PET scans for biomarkers of Alzheimer’s disease. These included 3 male patients and 16 female patients. All patients were diagnosed with probable Alzheimer’s disease according to the National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer’s Association guidelines, and all patients had a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score < 14/30 at baseline to be eligible for the study. We also included 19 healthy controls with an MMSE score greater than 26/30, no memory symptoms, no signs of dementia, and no other significant diseases. This group comprised 2 healthy male controls and 17 healthy female controls. Patients and healthy normal volunteers were between 60 and 95 years of age, had not taken antibiotics within two months, and had no serious metabolic diseases. Blood and fecal samples were collected in the morning after an overnight fast. Centrifuge at 4 °C and 3000 rpm for 10 min to obtain serum samples. Serum and fecal samples were carefully collected in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until analysis. Only serum samples without hemolysis were selected for testing. All gave informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by our local institutional ethics committee. Mice AD mouse model-5XFAD mice from Jackson Laborator (number 006554). These transgenic mice overexpress both human APP (695) harboring the Swedish (K670N, M671L), Florida (I716V), and London (V717I) FAD mutations and PS1 harboring the two FAD mutations M146L and L286V. Expression of both trans genes is regulated by neuronal-specific elements of the mouse Thy1 promoter. We cross-bred 5 × FAD mice with C57BL/6 J mice for more than 10 generations. Wild-type (WT) SPF C57BL/6 J littermates (The female parent of the first generation was provided by the YisiExperimental Animal Center, Changchun, China) were raised in the Experimental Animal Center of Zhongkai University of Agriculture and Engineering and served as controls. This experiment was conducted using female mice. All mice were housed in groups (2–5 mice per cage) in ventilated cages (Super Mouse 750, Lab Products) in a range of 30–70% unless a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle (06:00 light) was specified at 21–23 °C and 45–55% relative humidity. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. All animal experiments were approved by the Zhongkai University of Agriculture and Engineering. For experimental mice, SPF, and 5 × FAD mice were transferred and maintained in sterilized cages, fed an autoclaved 5010 PicoLab rodent diet (LadDiet), and provided with autoclaved drinking water. The 5 × FAD mice used in this study were behaviorally tested at 22 weeks of age. The exclusion criteria include abnormal weight and abnormal behavior (movement disorder and swimming disorder). The SPF mice used for comparison with the 5 × FAD mice were age-matched. All experiments were performed under the approval of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee the at Zhongkai University of Agriculture and Engineering. Sodium propionate treatment Adult mice (14 weeks) were treated with sodium propionate for 8 weeks. In the sodium propionate treatment experiment, mice were provided with drinking water containing sodium propionate (400 mmol/L) or sodium chloride as the control. Thirty-two mice were randomly divided into four groups: the control group, control sodium propionate group, 5 × FAD group, and 5 × FAD + sodium propionate group. Addition of sodium propionate to drinking water in 5 × FAD mice one month before the onset of cognitive dysfunction (3.5 months of age). Drinking water supplemented with sodium propionate for two months. Fecal samples were collected fresh at the end of each experiment. All mice underwent behavioral testing, and SP administration was maintained throughout the behavioral testing. Mice were euthanized with pentobarbital and sodium phenytoin (Euthasol, 180 mg kg , Virbac) and cardiac puncture was performed to collect blood samples. Blood samples kept at room temperature for 1 h to ensure complete clotting before centrifugation at 4 °C and 3000 rpm for 10 min to obtain serum samples. Tissues and Fecal were carefully collected in liquid nitrogen and then stored at − 80 °C until analysis. Cerebrospinal fluid collection Mice were anesthetized and positioned prone on the stereotaxic instrument. A sagittal incision was made in the skin beneath the occiput. With the aid of a dissection microscope, the subcutaneous tissue and neck muscles along the midline were carefully separated. A microretractor was then employed to hold the muscles apart. Subsequently, the mouse was positioned so that its body formed a 135° angle with the fixed head. At this angle, the dura and spinal medulla were visible, exhibiting a distinct glistening appearance, and allowing for observation of circulatory pulsations in the medulla and adjacent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space. The dura was penetrated using a 6-cm-long glass capillary with a tapered tip, measuring 0.5 mm in outer diameter. Upon encountering a discernible change in resistance during capillary insertion, CSF began to flow into the capillary. On average, approximately 8 μl of CSF was collected from each sample. All samples were promptly stored in polypropylene tubes at –80 °C until the time of injection. Cell culture and assay HT22 cells (a generous gift from Jilin University) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco,11,965,118) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, 10,091,148) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco,15,140,122). Cells were maintained at a confluency of less than 80% in 5% CO 2 at 37 °C. Digest the culture medium with 0.25% trypsin for 30–60 s during the passaging, after which the cells were inoculated with complete DMEM medium. The cells were then inoculated with complete DMEM medium in 25cm cell culture flasks and incubated in a 37 °C incubator. Cell morphology and medium color were observed every other day and the medium was changed. Human cerebrovascular endothelial cells HBMEC, human cerebrovascular pericytes HBVP, and astrocytes were cultured as above, and blood–brain barrier in vitro Transwell models were established using the above three cells, The models were assessed by trans-endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements using an epithelial voltammeter [ 94 ]. Aβ 25–35 (synthesized by Shanghai Sangon Biological Engineering Technology & Services Co) was diluted in distilled water at a concentration of 16 mmol/L and was maintained at 37 °C for 7 days to preage the peptide. Cells were starved for 4 h and then pretreated with propionate (5 mM) for 2 h before Aβ 25–35 was added. RNA or protein from cells was extracted after 24 h. Each experiment was repeated three times. The ATP concentration in HT22 cells was detected by an assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The measurement of ATP concentration was performed according to the instructions of the manufacturer. Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) Assay ROS level was detected by the assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). When HT22 cells grew to about 70%, the cells were collected in EP tubes, incubated with DCFH-DA for 20 min, and washed three times with DMEM without serum. The measurement of ROS level was performed following the instructions of the manufacturer. Sodium propionate treatment concentration screening The CCK-8 cell viability assay kit was used to screen the safe concentration of sodium propionate (C0042, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China). When the cell growth reached 60% confluency in a 96-well plate, the cell culture medium was replaced with FBS-free DMEM high-glucose medium for a 12-h treatment, allowing all cells to be synchronized in the same cell cycle phase. Subsequently, the medium was replaced with DMEM medium containing 10% FBS to achieve sodium propionate concentrations of 0–50 mM and 0–10 mM, respectively and incubated for 24 h. The medium was then replaced with 100 μL of fresh medium containing 10% CCK-8 reagent per well and incubated in a 37 °C cell culture incubator for 2 h. The 96-well plate was then removed and the absorbance was measured at 450 nm using an ELISA reader. Bacterial culture Akkermansia muciniphila ATCC BAA-835 was cultured from –80 °C according to ATCC culture guidelines, screened on BD Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) agar supplemented with 0.4% mucin (Sigma), and incubated at 37 °C under anaerobic conditions (5% H 2 , 10% CO 2 , rest N 2 ), and the A. muciniphila were given resuspended in anaerobic PBS prior to dosing and mice were gavaged at a concentration of 4 × 10 CFU/mL (once every two days). RNA interference a. In vivo RNA interference: Slow viruses of shRNA-GPR41 (1.93 × 10 TU/ml), shRNA-GPR43 (2.60 × 10 TU/ml), and shRNA-control (2.30 × 10 TU/ml) were injected into the dentate gyrus (DG) of hippocampus of 5 × FAD or WT mice (2.5 months old) under 1% pentobarbital anesthesia. The mice were placed in a stereotaxic apparatus, their heads were shaved, and the skin was disinfected. A small hole was drilled above the injection site. The microinjection needle was slowly inserted into the target area and rested for 5 min before injection. According to the mouse brain stereotaxic atlas, 0.05 μl of slow virus was slowly injected into the bilateral hippocampal DG area, relative to the Bregma coordinates as follows: anterior–posterior = −1.75 mm from bregma; lateral = ± 1.47 mm; depth = 2.45 mm. The injection time for each side was 5 min, and the needle was left in place for 5 min before slowly being withdrawn. The sham group was injected with an equal amount of empty virus. All procedures were performed under sterile conditions, and the skin incision was treated with penicillin for antibacterial purposes, and the wound was sutured. The mice were given carprofen (5 mg/kg) before and during the surgery, as well as 24 h after the surgery to minimize discomfort. b. In vitro RNA interference: The infection method of slow virus interference vectors of GPR41 and GPR43 was carried out according to the instructions of Shanghai Sangon Biotech. HT22 cells were grown overnight in a six-well plate (2 × 10 cells/well), infected with MOI = 5 and cultured for 24 h. GFP-positive cells were monitored under a fluorescence microscope. shRNA lentiviruses were purchased from Sangon Biotech. Behavioral tests Behavioral measurements were performed in the following order: Nest building, Open field, Novel object recognition test, Elevated plus-maze test, Morris water maze. Morris water maze Behavioral assessment was performed as previously describe [ 95 ]. In brief, experiments were performed in a 120-cm diameter, 50-cm deep tank filled with opacified water kept at 20 ± 1 °C. The tank was equipped with a 10-cm diameter platform submerged 1 cm under the water’s surface. Spatial cues were placed on the wall in the water-maze. Training consisted of daily sessions for 5 consecutive days. Mice in WT, WT + SP, 5 × FAD and 5 × FAD + SP groups were trained 4 times daily. The start positions varied pseudorandomly among the 4 cardinal points. Mean intertrial interval was 90 min. Mice in WT, WT + Akkermansia muciniphila , 5 × FAD, and 5 × FAD + Akkermansia muciniphila groups were trained 1 time daily. The start position is in the opposite quadrant of the quadrant where the platform is located. Each trial ended when the animal reached the platform. A 90-s cut-off was used, after which mice were gently guided to the platform. The exploration period was: 24 h after the last training, following which the platform was removed from the pool. All mice were tested for 60 s. Animals were video-tracked using Flyde (Guangzhou Feidi Biotechnology, China) and behavioral parameters (swim speed, traveled distance, latency, percentage of time in each quadrant, percentage of distance in each quadrant) were automatically calculated. Elevated plus-maze test The elevated plus-maze test was conducted following standard procedures. The apparatus used (EB Instrument) consisted of two open arms (35 × 5 cm), two enclosed arms (35 × 5 × 15 cm), and a central square platform (5 × 5 cm), positioned 45 cm above the ground. Each mouse was placed on the central platform, facing the same open arm, and allowed to explore for a total of 5 min. During this time, the number of entries into both the open and closed arms, as well as the duration spent in each, were recorded. The percentage of time spent in the open arms was calculated by dividing the time spent in open arms by the total time. Open field test Testing was performed as previously described [ 96 ]. Each mouse was placed near the edge of a 35 × 42 cm open-field arena, which was segmented into 25 squares, with the central area comprising 9 squares and the remainder forming the periphery. The mouse’s movements were recorded for 5 min using a camera. The video footage was later analyzed using EthoVision XT 7.0 software (Noldus). Between trials, the arena was disinfected with 75% ethanol. Both the open field test and other behavioral assessments were conducted under dim lighting conditions. Novel object recognition test Testing was performed as previously described [ 97 ]. Each trial consisted of two phases: a familiarization session and a test session. During familiarization, each mouse was placed in a 45 × 45 × 30 cm testing arena with light levels in the center adjusted to 100 ± 5 lx to minimize anxiety. The mouse was given 5 min to freely explore two identical objects (5 × 5 × 5 cm) positioned diagonally across the arena. Twenty-four hours later, one of the familiar objects was replaced with a novel object of similar size but different color, shape, and texture. In the test session, the mouse was again allowed 5 min to explore both objects. Mice that retained memory of the familiar object typically spent more time interacting with the novel one. Mouse activity was tracked using the Flyde system (Guangzhou Feidi Biotechnology, China), and exploration time was recorded when the mouse’s snout was within 2 cm of the object. The exploration index was calculated as the time spent exploring both objects relative to the total session time, while the discrimination index was calculated as the time spent exploring the novel object relative to the combined exploration of both objects during the test session. Nest building Several uniformly sized unscented paper towels were placed in the cage 1 h before the onset of the nightly rhythm. Several photos were taken 15 min before the activity period to assess nesting behavior. Scoring criteria (total 5 points) include: (1) Paper towels intact (100%); (2) Paper towels mostly intact (> 90% intact); (3) Paper towels mostly shredded (< 90%), but not Identifiable nest location (flat if there is a nest); (4) The paper towel is torn and there are obvious nests (> 90%, paper towel) The towels are arranged in a certain direction and the nest is flat); (5) An almost perfect nest (the nest can completely surround the mouse). SCFAs measurements Testing was performed as previously described [ 98 ]. To prepare the stock solution, 0.1250 g each of acetic acid, propionic acid, isobutyric acid, n-butyric acid, isovaleric acid, and n-valeric acid were dissolved in a 100 mL volumetric flask with ether. For sample preparation, 1 mL, 0.75 mL, 0.5 mL, and 0.25 mL aliquots of the stock solution were taken and diluted to 100 mL with ether in separate volumetric flasks. The samples were then analyzed, and a standard curve was generated. To process the samples, 2 mL of a 1:3 phosphoric acid aqueous solution was added, followed by vortex mixing for 2 min. Ether (1 mL) was added for extraction, and the mixture was left to stand for 10 min before centrifuging at 4000 rpm for 20 min (in an ice water bath for low-temperature processing). A second 1 mL of ether was added, followed by another 10-min extraction and centrifugation at the same speed. The two extracts were combined, concentrated to a volume of 1 mL, and subjected to analysis. Quantification of SCFAs was performed using a GCMS ISQ LT system (Thermo Scientific, USA), equipped with an auto-injector and a flame ionization detector. The separation was achieved on a DB-FFAP capillary column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 µm). The sample was injected with a 60:1 split ratio. The injection port temperature was set to 250 °C. The column temperature was initially maintained at 80 °C for 2 min, then raised to 150 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min for 2 min, and further increased to 180 °C at 15 °C/min for 5 min, with a total runtime of 18 min. Helium (99.999%) served as the carrier gas with a flow rate of 3 mL/min. The MS was operated in electron impact mode at 70 eV, with an ion source temperature of 230 °C and an interface temperature of 250 °C. The solvent delay time was 1 min, and data acquisition was performed in selected ion monitoring mode with a scan interval of 0.3 s. Tissue sample collection and perfusion The mice were deeply anesthetized (EEG flattened) and killed (heart rate and respiration decreased to zero) by intraperitoneal injection of a mixture of pentobarbital and sodium phenytoin (Euthasol, 180 mg/kg, Virbac). Mouse tissues for doing real-time PCR and Western blotting were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and kept at –80 °C before use. Mice used to perform immunofluorescence assays were perfused with saline through the heart and then perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffer. The brains were then dissected on dry ice, the hippocampus was removed and incubated in phosphate buffer with 30% sucrose. The tissues were then placed on dry ice and embedded in an optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound (Tissue-Tek). Mice used for transmission electron microscopy were perfused with a mixture of buffer (pH 7.35) containing 1.5% paraformaldehyde and 1.5% glutaraldehyde via the heart, while 1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm hippocampal tissue squares were later fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde. Alcian blue staining Colon samples stored in methanol were embedded in paraffin and sectioned at 5 μm thickness. The sections were first deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated with distilled water. They were then incubated in alcian blue solution for 30 min, followed by a 2-min rinse under running tap water. After rinsing with distilled water, the sections were dehydrated twice and treated with absolute alcohol twice for 3 min each. Finally, the sections were cleared in xylene three times for 3 min each, after which a cover glass was mounted. Real-time PCR Cultured cell or mouse tissue was stored in RNAlater (Ambion) or directly transferred to TRIzol (Invitrogen). The extracted RNA was quantified using Nano Drop and 2000 ng of RNA was used to prepare the reverse transcription reaction system in RNase-free PCR tubes. The reaction mixture included 5 × HiScript II Buffer (4 μL), HiScript II (Vazyme, R2223) Reverse Transcriptase (1 μL) and ddH2O to a total volume of 20 μL. The reaction was carried out using the following program: 25 °C for 5 min, 50 °C for 15 min and 85 °C for 2 min, resulting in cDNA synthesis. For qPCR, the reaction mixture consisted of 2 × PerfectStart Green qPCR Super Mix (10 μL) (TransGen Biotech, AQ601), forward primer (0.4 μL), reverse primer (0.4 μL) and template (cDNA diluted 10 times from the above RT-PCR, 9.2 μL). The amplification program included the following steps: 94 °C for 30 s, 94 °C for 5 s, 55 °C for 15 s and 72 °C for 10 s (repeated for 40 cycles from the second to the fourth step). Gene expression results are expressed as arbitrary units relative to the expression of the housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH). Primer sequences are as follows: Synaptophysin: 5′- CCACTGACCCAGAGAACATTAT −3′ and 5′- CTTGAACACGAACCATAGGTTG-3′; GPR41: 5′- AGTCGCCTGGTGTGGATACTGAG −3′ and 5′- GCCGAAGCAGACGAAGAAGATGAG-3′; GPR43: 5′- GCTGACAGGCTTCGGCTTCTAC −3′ and 5′- CAGAGCAGCGATCACTCCATACAG-3′; PSD-95: 5′- ATGTGCTTCATGTAATTGACGC −3′ and 5′- TTTAACCTTGACCACTCTCGTC-3′; LC3: 5′- CCACCAAGATCCCAGTGATTAT −3′ and 5′- TGATTATCTTGATGAGCTCGCT-3′. PGC1α: 5′- GGATATACTTTACGCAGGTCGA −3′ and 5′- CGTCTGAGTTGGTATCTAGGTC-3′. Opa1: 5′- CTTACATGCAGAATC CTAACGC −3′ and 5′- CCAAGTCTGTAACAATACTGCG −3′. Fis1: 5′- CCTGGTTCGAAGCAAATACAAT −3′ and 5′- CTTTTCATATTCCTTGAGCCGG-3′. Drp1: 5′- ACTGATTCAATCCGTGATGAGT −3′ and 5′- GTAACCTATTCAGGGTCCTAGC-3′. Western blotting method Cultured cell or mouse tissue samples were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline and subsequently lysed. Protein extracts were separated on 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gels, transferred to nitrocellulose membranes, and stained with antibodies against Parkin (Abcam, ab77924, dilution 1:2000), Drp1 (Abcam, ab184247, dilution 1:1000), Pink 1 (Proteintech, 23,274–1-AP, dilution 1:1000) were stained with antibodies. β-actin antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, 4970, dilution 1:1000) was used as a loading control. The blots were then detected with the corresponding secondary antibody (Cell Signaling, 7074, dilution 1:3000) labeled with horseradish peroxidase. Band intensities were observed by chemiluminescence using the Pierce ECL 2 Western Blotting Substrate Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Immunofluorescence staining assays Immunofluorescence (IF) staining was performed as previously described. In brief, cells or tissue sections grown on slides were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min and treated with 0.5% TritonX-100 for 5 min, blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin for 120 min, and stained with anti-Drp1 (Abcam, ab184247, dilution 1:250), anti-Parkin (Abcam, ab77924, dilution 1:250), anti-Pink 1 (Proteintech, 23,274–1-AP, dilution 1:250) and anti-TOMM20 (Abcam, ab283317, dilution 1:500), respectively. Slides were washed and then incubated with Dylight-594 Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (H + L) (Abbkine) and Dylight-488 Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) (Abbkine). Nuclei were stained with 4′, 6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; Beyotime). 16S rRNA gene sequencing and analysis Testing was performed as previously described [ 99 ]. In short, the V4 hypervariable region of the 16S rRNA genes was amplified in duplicate. The resulting products were purified using Agencourt AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter, CA, USA) and quantified using the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Life Technologies, CA, USA). Illumina sequencing adapters, along with dual-index barcodes, were appended to the purified amplicons using a limited cycle PCR approach with the Nextera XT Index Kit (Illumina, CA, USA). Amplicons from 96 samples, including controls, were pooled in equimolar ratios. The pooled libraries were further purified via gel extraction, followed by quantification using Qiagen reagents (Germany). Sequencing was conducted on an Illumina MiSeq platform, employing 300-bp paired-end reads with v3 chemistry. After sequencing, the raw reads were de-multiplexed, pre-processed, merged, and quality-filtered using the DADA2 pipeline. Primer sequences were removed using a custom Python script, and reads were truncated at 250 bp. Taxonomic assignments were made with a modified SILVA reference database. Only samples containing at least 2,000 reads were included in subsequent analyses. To validate and enrich taxonomic classifications, representative sequences from each amplicon sequence variant were subjected to BLAST searches against the NCBI non-redundant protein and 16S rRNA gene sequence databases. Permeability analysis of the brain-blood barrier (BBB) The permeability of the BBB was assessed by the efflux of Evans blue (EB) dye. Evans blue dye 2% (30 mg/kg) was injected through the tail vein and allowed to circulate for 120 min. Under animal anesthesia, cardiac blood collection and PBS cardiac perfusion were performed, followed by removal of the brain. The blood was centrifuged at 3500 RPM for 15 min, the supernatant was aspirated, and the brain samples were homogenized in formamide. Homogenized brain samples were incubated overnight at 55 °C and then centrifuged at 12,000 RPM for 45 min. The absorbance of Evans Blue at 620 nm was measured for the supernatant and serum using a spectrophotometer (GENESYS 10S UV–Vis spectrophotometer; Thermo Electron Corporation, Madison, WI). MitoTracker Each vial of MitoTracker® Red CMXRos contains 50 µg of lyophilized solid. To make a 1 mM stock solution, this solid needs to be dissolved in 94.1 µL of high-quality DMSO. The HT22 cell stock solution was diluted directly into the growth medium at a concentration of 150 nM and incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. After incubation, cells are fixed in ice-cold methanol at –20 °C for 15 min and then rinsed three times with PBS for 5 min each. Observe under an inverted fluorescence microscope. Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) For conventional TEM analysis, the cells were harvested and washed with PBS three times, followed by 0.1 M CAB buffer, pH 7.2 twice. Subsequently, the cells were treated with fixative I (2.5% GA and 4% PFA in 0.1 M CAB buffer, pH 7.2) at RT for 2 h. After washing with 0.1 M CAB buffer three times (each time for 5 min), the cells were incubated with fixative II (1% OsO4 in 0.1 M CAB pH 7.2, 15 mg/mL K4[Fe (CN)6]) at RT for 1 h, followed by two washes with 0.1 M CAB buffer and three washes with double-distilled water (ddH 2 O). Then, the cells were incubated with 0.4% uranyl acetate at 4 °C for 1 h. After extensive washing with ddH 2 O, the cells were dehydrated in a graded series of ethanol and embedded in Spurr’s resin according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The embedded samples were trimmed and sectioned to 70 nm thickness by an EMUC7 ultramicrotome (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany). The cell sections were stained with 0.4% uranyl acetate at RT for 20 min and then incubated with 4% lead citrate solution for 6 min. Electron micrographs were obtained with a Talos F200S transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Experimental design No statistical methods were used to predefine sample size. All animals were randomly assigned to treatment groups using random list generator at random.org. Samples from all groups were processed at the same time and using identical techniques. For all animal experiments, groups were labeled by number for analyses and were only decoded after data analysis. Monitoring of mice was done with blinding. Quantification and statistical analysis Data were expressed as the mean ± standard error of the means. Unless otherwise indicated individual dots represent each individual mouse. Data were analyzed with independent samples t-test or by One-way ANOVA / Two-way ANOVA via the GraphPad Prism8 software can be found in the figures’ legend. One-way ANOVA of variance used Tukey post hoc tests. Two-way ANOVA correction for multiple comparisons was performed using the Holm–Šídák method or Tukey’s post hoc test where appropriate. Significance is defined as: * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001. title: Identifying gut microbiota with high specificity for ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion

Abstract Gut microbiota can regulate the metabolic and immunological aspects of ischemic stroke and modulate the treatment effects. The present study aimed to identify specific changes in gut microbiota in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) ischemic stroke and assess the potential association between gut microbiota and clinical features of ischemic stroke. A total of 63 CSVD patients, 64 cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) patients, and 36 matching normal controls (NCs) were included in this study. The fecal samples were collected for all participants and analyzed for gut microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing technology. The abundances of five gut microbiota, including genera Bifidobacterium, Butyricimonas, Blautia, and Dorea and species Bifidobacterium_longum, showed significant changes with high specificity in the LVO patients as compared to the NCs and CSVD patients. In LVO patients, the genera Bifidobacterium and Blautia and species Bifidobacterium_longum were significantly correlated with the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) scores at the admission and discharge of the patients. Serum triglyceride levels could significantly affect the association of the abundance of genus Bifidobacterium and species Bifidobacterium_longum with the NIHSS scores at admission and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at discharge in LVO patients. The identification of five gut microbiota with high specificity were identified in the early stage of LVO stroke, which contributed to performed an effective clinical management for LVO ischemic stroke.
